vignette:
Amir presents as a man meticulously composed, a skill honed over three decades in public service. In his tailored suit, he commands a room with a quiet authority that his constituents find reassuring. At 64, he is a respected city councilman, known for his fierce advocacy for infrastructure projects and his unyielding focus on budgetary details. He speaks of concrete and rebar, of zoning laws and fiscal responsibility, with a passion that seems to leave little room for anything else. It is in the quiet moments, when the cameras are off and the aides have gone home, that the carefully constructed architecture of his life reveals its cracks.

It began nearly forty years ago. He was a young man then, just 25, full of an idealistic fervor that led him to a dusty, war-torn village as a relief worker with an international NGO. He wasn't a soldier; he was there to distribute food and medical supplies. He remembers the heat, the constant hum of flies, and the faces of the children, so resilient in their play. The event itself didn't arrive with a dramatic crescendo but with a sudden, indifferent whistle that sliced through the afternoon air. He had been handing a small boy a bag of rice when the mortar struck the marketplace.

The world dissolved into a storm of sound and pressure. When his hearing returned, it was to the symphony of screaming. He doesn't remember making a choice, only moving through the thick, acrid smoke, his body acting on some primal instinct. What haunts him is not the grand scale of the carnage, but the fragments. A woman's brightly colored headscarf lying in a pool of blood. The smell of scorched sugar from an overturned vendor's cart. And most vividly, the image of the small boy he had just been helping, or rather, the small, bright red toy truck that lay on its side near a crater, its wheels still spinning slowly. He never saw the boy again.

He returned home a month later, a ghost in his own life. He threw himself into his studies, then into a law career, and finally into politics. He found a strange comfort in the rigid predictability of parliamentary procedure, in the black-and-white text of a bill. It was a world of rules and consequences, a universe away from the random, senseless violence that had unmade him. He married, had two children, and built a life that looked successful from the outside.

But his wife, Lena, had once called him a ghost. "You're here, Amir," she'd said, years before she finally left, her voice cracking, "but you never really came home." He hadn't known how to explain that home was the one place he couldn't find. Sleep offered no refuge; he would often wake up drenched in sweat, his heart hammering against his ribs, the scent of dust and iron in his nostrils. During the day, he was a master of control, but a car backfiring on the street below his office could send a jolt of pure terror through him, leaving him breathless and disoriented for minutes.

He avoids the news, a difficult feat for a politician. When images of foreign conflicts flash across the screen in the lobby, he feels a cold fist clench in his gut and will turn abruptly to his aide, asking a sharp, irrelevant question about zoning permits, his voice a shield. He is emotionally distant from his adult children, loving them from an academic remove he cannot seem to bridge. He feels a pervasive, low-grade guilt, a sense that he, the one who survived, is an imposter in his own life. He carries the weight of it not as a memory, but as a debt. A debt to a small boy whose face he can no longer fully picture, but whose little red truck he sees with perfect, devastating clarity.
